query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Sputter-depositing a thin CrN film on boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment compared to uncoated borides.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components that, in their as-fabricated state, are vulnerable to direct molten-aluminum attack and interfacial degradation during hot-dip plating.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, adherent CrN coating (potentially with a pre-sputtered Cr buffer layer) via sputtering on the surface of the boride component.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective under typical plating conditions (e.g., high temperature exposure to molten aluminum over repeated plating cycles) provided that the CrN film remains intact and adherent under thermal cycling and mechanical stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The deposited CrN layer forms a dense columnar microstructure that limits molten-aluminum wetting, reduces interdiffusion, and acts as a physical/chemical barrier between the aggressive aluminum environment and the underlying boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: By preventing direct contact between the molten aluminum and the boride substrate, the CrN coating limits the penetration and reactive dissolution processes that normally lead to corrosion. The coating’s low wetting angle with aluminum minimizes film formation along the interface and thereby reduces subsequent corrosion damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a bare boride surface, the CrN-coated component is predicted to have a lower rate of corrosion (assessed by reduced weight loss and lower electrochemical corrosion current densities) when exposed to molten aluminum. The improvement is expected to be significant yet its precise magnitude will depend on the coating thickness and process parameters.
generation.baseline: Untreated boride components in the same hot-dip aluminum-plating environment, which typically exhibit higher mass loss and surface degradation due to molten aluminum attack.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is likely limited by the coating’s integrity; if the CrN film is compromised by mechanical wear or severe thermal cycling, its effectiveness may diminish. In addition, the operating temperature must be within the thermal stability range of the CrN coating.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (e.g., percentage reduction in corrosion rate) is uncertain and will depend on optimal deposition conditions, coating thickness, and long-term exposure conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical sets of boride-based component samples. Apply a sputtered CrN film (with an optimized Cr buffer layer if needed) on one set while leaving the other set untreated as a control. Subject both sets to identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions (temperature, time, flow dynamics) that simulate hot-dip plating. After exposure, compare corrosion performance by measuring weight loss, electrochemical responses, and surface morphology.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance/corrosion current densities (via potentiodynamic polarization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrN-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion (i.e., lower mass loss, fewer degradation features, and improved electrochemical parameters) relative to the untreated samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Improvement of Corrosion and Wear Resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 Medium-Entropy Alloy by Sputtering CrN Film

Abstract: In this study, Co, Cr, and Ni were selected as the equal-atomic medium entropy alloy (MEA) systems, and Si was added to form CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA. In order to further improve its wear and corrosion properties, CrN film was sputtered on the surface. In addition, to enhance the adhesion between the soft CoCrNiSi0.3 substrate and the super-hard CrN film, a Cr buffer layer was pre-sputtered on the CoCrNiSi0.3 substrate. The experimental results show that the CrN film exhibits a columnar grain structure, and the film growth rate is about 2.022 μm/h. With the increase of sputtering time, the increase in CrN film thickness, and the refinement of columnar grains, the wear and corrosion resistance improves. Among all CoCrNiSi0.3 MEAs without and with CrN films prepared in this study, the CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA with 3 h-sputtered CrN film has the lowest wear rate of 2.249 × 10−5 mm3·m−1·N−1, and the best corrosion resistance of Icorr 19.37 μA·cm–2 and Rp 705.85 Ω·cm2.
